chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who marries off his son while he is a minor. He said, 'There is no harm.' I said, 'Does the father's divorce (of the son) take effect?' He said, 'No.' I said, 'Upon whom is the dowry?' He said, 'Upon the father, if he guaranteed it for them; and if he did not guarantee it, then it is upon the boy, unless the boy has no wealth, in which case the father is responsible for him even if he did not guarantee it.' And he said, 'When a man marries off his son, it is up to the son (to accept or reject); but when he marries off his daughter, it takes effect.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And if a father and a grandfather are present for the marriage contract of the daughter, the grandfather is more entitled (to contract it); but if the father precedes with the contract, the grandfather has no right to object. (1560)
36. To indicate this, what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated - from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'A girl, her father wants to marry her to a man, and her grandfather wants to marry her to another man.' He said, 'The grandfather is more entitled to that, provided it is not detrimental, if the father has not married her off before him, and the marriage of the father and the grandfather is valid upon her.'
ai.seo_question: Who has the primary right to contract the marriage of a daughter, the father or the grandfather, according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* delineates the hierarchy of marriage guardianship (*wilayah*), establishing that while a father’s contract for a minor daughter is binding, the grandfather holds priority unless the father has already acted. It further distinguishes between the autonomy of a minor son, who may ratify or reject the marriage upon maturity, and the financial liability for the bride price (*mahr*), which falls on the father if he guaranteed it or on the son otherwise. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on the father’s primary role in female guardianship while acknowledging the grandfather’s secondary right to ensure the daughter’s best interest.
